rows.verified: A confined space is enclosed or largely enclosed and has a reasonably foreseeable specified risk such as fire, explosion, loss of consciousness, asphyxiation or drowning.
Entry to a confined space should be avoided where the work can be completed from outside.
If confined-space entry is unavoidable, the particular hazards and risks must be assessed before work begins.
Harmful fumes should be removed or controlled, including by suitable ventilation where appropriate.
Where liquids or gases could enter the space, isolation measures such as locking valves shut should be considered.
Where oxygen is insufficient, breathing apparatus or effective ventilation is required before entry.
Adequate emergency arrangements must be in place before confined-space work starts.
Emergency planning must provide a way to monitor and rescue workers and must not rely only on the emergency services.
Controls depend on the space, atmosphere, contents, isolation, work method, worker competence and rescue arrangements.
Confined-space evidence is space-, task- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level fatality or exposure probability.
Employers must assess risks to employees from noise at work.
Employers must take action to reduce noise exposure that creates health or safety risks.
Hearing protection must be provided where exposure cannot be reduced sufficiently by other methods.
Employers must ensure that legal noise exposure limits are not exceeded.
Employees must receive information, instruction and training about workplace-noise risks and controls.
Health surveillance is required where workplace noise presents a risk to health.
The lower exposure action values are 80 dB(A) daily or weekly exposure and 135 dB(C) peak sound pressure.
The upper exposure action values are 85 dB(A) daily or weekly exposure and 137 dB(C) peak sound pressure.
Noise controls depend on measured exposure, peak levels, duration, frequency content, work patterns and individual susceptibility.
Workplace-noise evidence is exposure- and task-specific and is not an exact parcel-level hearing-loss probability.
